family_judgments.evidence: The two short-text and transformation items are invalid under their narrow answer keys, whereas the MCQ is determinately scoreable; this prevents equivalent measurement evidence across formats.
All formats retain present-perfect formation, present agreement, and polar-question inversion as the intended grammar; MCQ changes response mechanism rather than the KC definition.
Every format concerns Alex asking whether Maya has completed packing the same picnic basket.

criteria.evidence: The blank requires present HAVE agreement (Has), participle packed, and operator-first question order.
The object and lexical material are simple; no important grammar beyond the declared perfect, present finite form, and polar-question operations is required.
The supplied lemma and subject do not supply either the auxiliary or participial form, so the declared operations remain necessary.
“Has Maya already packed” also completes the context naturally; the instruction does not say to use only the supplied words.
The reasonable completion “Has Maya already packed” is unaccepted; omission makes a grammatically correct response fail exact-match scoring.
Picnic-basket vocabulary and the completion context are transparent for B2 learners.
Producing the turn requires Has + Maya + packed, activating all three declared operations.
The dialogue introduces no material grammatical dependency outside the target construction.
Neither inversion nor the auxiliary/participle sequence is supplied in the response slot.
“Has Maya already packed the picnic basket?” is a natural question in this completion-now context.
The reasonable unkeyed completion “Has Maya already packed” is excluded despite yielding a correct question.
The short dialogue is semantically clear and does not add substantial pragmatic burden.
Selecting A requires distinguishing agreement, participial form, and standard inversion from the targeted distractors.
All options use the same simple lexical frame; the later-completion meaning is explicit.
As a recognition task, testwise elimination of visibly ill-formed B/C can reduce evidence for independently constructing the full target, though A still contrasts with uninverted D.
Given “standard question,” A is the uniquely appropriate option; D is marked declarative intonation rather than the requested standard written form.
A is the sole keyed option and no solver-proposed unkeyed alternative requires adjudication.
The options and context impose little lexical or discourse burden.
The learner must construct present perfect auxiliary agreement, participle, and inversion in a full question.
The supplied lexical frame controls vocabulary while leaving the declared grammatical operations active.
The cue supplies lemmas and content words but not Has or packed, and does not give an already formed question.
“Has Maya already packed the picnic basket?” and “Has Maya finished packing the picnic basket?” are contextually natural ways to ask about completion.
Natural full-sentence alternatives such as “Has Maya already packed the picnic basket?” are unaccepted; the prompt does not prohibit the optional adverb.
The source situation is simple and maintains the same participants and event.

summary: The target construction is active and semantically matched, but the production items reject natural optional “already” variants, a blocking response-coverage defect.
